title: Navaratri: nine nights of the Goddess
hook: Durga meets the buffalo demon; nine nights of dancing, and on the tenth day the good wins

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ganesh Chaturthi, a clay god welcomed home and given back to the water. Welcome it, then let it go.

Eleven at night in Gujarat, and an open ground is packed. People in mirrored skirts and embroidered jackets move in huge circles, clapping, spinning, sticks clicking in rhythm. They'll be back tomorrow night, and the night after: nine nights in a row. Far to the east, in Bengal, neighborhoods build glittering temporary halls for a ten-armed goddess on a lion. In the south, families set out steps of dolls. Different places, different customs, the same nine nights. And at the center of many of them, one story: a demon nobody could defeat, and the Goddess who did.
screen: `NINE NIGHTS OF DANCING.` → `A TEN-ARMED GODDESS ON A LION.` → `A DEMON NOBODY COULD DEFEAT.`

segments.voice: The story comes from the Devi Mahatmya, the Glory of the Goddess, a Sanskrit text recited in homes and temples during these nights. Mahishasura, a demon who is part buffalo, grows so powerful that he drives the gods out of heaven. In a popular telling, he'd won a boon that no man or god could kill him. The gods are so furious that their anger bursts out of them as light, and the light of every god flows together into one blazing form: a woman. The Goddess. Each god hands her a weapon: Shiva's trident, Vishnu's discus, and a lion to ride. People call her Durga, the one who is hard to reach, hard to defeat. She rides out laughing, and the battle begins. Mahishasura keeps changing shape to escape her: a buffalo, a lion, a warrior with a sword, an elephant, a buffalo again. She meets every form. Finally, as he struggles half out of the buffalo's body, she puts her foot on his neck and ends it. That's why images of Durga so often show her spear in a buffalo. Navaratri means nine nights: nava, nine, and ratri, night. Some honor nine forms of the Goddess, one each night. Some fast. Some dance the garba in her honor. The tenth day, Vijayadashami, the tenth of victory, is when the good wins. In much of north India it's also Dussehra, when Rama's victory over Ravana is celebrated with huge effigies of the ten-headed king going up in flames. Different regions tell the victory through different stories, and the festival brings each of them to the same tenth morning.
screen: `THE GODS' LIGHT BECOMES THE GODDESS.` · `DURGA MEETS EVERY FORM HE TAKES.` · `NAVA + RATRI: NINE NIGHTS.` · `THE TENTH DAY: THE GOOD WINS.`

segments.voice: Sit up tall, like someone riding a lion, and think of one small, ordinary thing that keeps changing shape on you: the urge to snap at someone, the scroll that eats your evening, the voice that says you're not enough. Notice how it shifts forms to get past you. Then calmly name it, and decide: not tonight, just for tonight.
Navaratri. Nava, nine; ratri, night. Nine nights of the Goddess, and on the tenth day, victory.
Your line: nine nights, then the dawn. The good gets the tenth day. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: During Navaratri, Hindus honor the Goddess over nine nights in regional ways: garba and dandiya dancing in Gujarat, Durga Puja in Bengal, displays of dolls (golu) in the south, fasting and recitation of the Devi Mahatmya in many homes; the tenth day, Vijayadashami or Dussehra, celebrates the victory of good.
